utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In the absence of Judge Mindua, Judge Harhoff and I sit pursuant to the provisions of Rule 15 bis. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness T-53, last time we began the examination-in-chief and you spoke about what you saw from the place from which you were looking at Pofalici. In addition to what you already said, you mentioned a friend of yours and his parents. How did this whole episode in Pofalici end, in terms of what you saw and what you learned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I saw with my own eyes was that the Serbian houses were set on fire, that it gradually moved to the hill above Pofalici. Later, I learned that a terrible crime had been committed there, that many residents of Pofalici were killed and that their bodies had not been found and buried to this date. I cited an example of the parents of a friend of mine about whom I know for sure that haven't been buried to this very day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How long did you stay in this place that you mentioned last time? If we can please have the map on the screens, the map that was shown to the witness last time. It's 65 ter 02829, and it already contains certain markings. So the map, 65 ter 02829.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Will it ever appear? Is there a problem? Because I don't see how we can wait much longer. Ah, it's here finally.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, last time you explained and put certain letters relating to something that you were asked about. Tell me, how long did you remain in these positions as a fighter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the 28th of May 1992 is the date by which I remained in this position.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell the Judges where did you move after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the 28th of May, 1992, due to certain circumstances, I started, so to speak, my service in the logistic organ of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, its technical service.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we now move into a private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In that respect, were you able to take any action on your own with respect to fuel, ammunition, et cetera? Who took care of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I, as an individual and as a desk officer in the technical service, was not able to do anything on my own initiative. Everybody knows what a desk officer is in charge of. However, due to the intelligence that indicated that the BH army was to launch attacks, meetings were held with company managers; that is to say the companies situated in the area of Serbian Sarajevo. They earmarked some money from the money they had in their accounts in order to procure and buy fuel for the units. The problem was that laws and regulations were in force saying that 30 per cent of the fuel should be allocated for other structures, and the corps was very far away where fuel was available.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us not leave aside now food and clothing. Let us concentrate on ammunition now. Did you find anything about what kind of requisition orders issued for ammunition?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The standard and usual communication with units was that units, based on their needs, would submit a request to the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, i.e. to the logistics organ of the command of the SRK.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know who was the person in charge, the main decision maker?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The requests received and processed by the logistics department for the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska were approved by the technical service of the Main Staff of Republika Srpska. The munition was stored in the depots of the 27 logistics base which was in charge of supplies of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and the Drina Corps of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Judges what kind of ammunition was available at the time in light of everything that you mentioned? Were there any problems in that respect?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were problems, but the Main Staff in most cases gave its approval for infantry ammunition. That was the time when the truce was in place and when the artillery was to be placed in the exclusion zone, I don't know at exactly what distance. Therefore, there was no need for artillery ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe you didn't understand me. What I meant was, at the time when you learned about the imminent attack, what happened after the attack at Zlatiste? What happened next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The attack on Zlatiste that took place some time in the latter part of May. From that moment on, it became obvious that units had to be replenished with fuel and ammunition. In that period the units received certain amounts of ammunition and fuel from the Main Staff and were more or less prepared to encounter the BH attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, do you know anything about - and I'm going to ask you this directly - about air bombs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some time in early June, requests kept coming in -- started -- correction, started coming in for air bombs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were you ever in a position to do something about this? You personally.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The requests were forwarded to the Main Staff of Republika Srpska army. At the time, I knew that there was no need for these type of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever see a report about these weapons being used some place -- somewhere, whether these air bombs were used?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reports on the use of ammunition, as a rule, were submitted to the operations organ. Sometimes they were submitted to the logistics organ as well. But I personally did not see these reports. Since the rears -- the logistics was in Pale and I was in Lukavica, I couldn't -- had no opportunity to see these reports. The consumption of the ammunition at that period was so minimal that there was no need for these reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you -- show you a document. You said that you arrived there in late December and you started working in early January. I'm going to show you a document and ask you whether perhaps you had an opportunity to see it, and it's 65 ter 03222.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, while we wait for this document to come up, could I ask the witness why he said that according to his evaluation, there was no need for these type of weapons? Speaking about the air bombs. Mr. Witness, why did you think that there was no need for these weapons? What was the basis for your estimation of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Sarajevo-Romanija Corps naturally didn't have aircraft or air force. There was no need, therefore, for air bombs. I have never seen an air bomb myself. It was not stored in depots of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. So I never had any contact with this type of ammunition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But were you aware of the possibility of launching these weapons from ground positions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't know that at the time. A month later, after the BH army commenced its attack on the units of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, at one point, while listening to the news of the BH federation or the Muslim radio, I don't know how it was called at the time, I heard, and there was a live programme on, and I heard a person who phoned in from Kosevo and who said that some kind of air bomb had dropped but that did not explode. After that, another person phoned in, I think he or she was living in Alipasino Polje and said that a bomb had dropped on Alipasino Polje, that there were no wounded people but that shrapnel were as big as buckets. That is the first time that I heard about air bombs. That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was sometime in early July 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, the document is on the screen so let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at this document? Did you perhaps ever see a document like this? And you can also take a look at who issued this document and what it pertains to. I'm not going to lead you about what this document is about. Can you please read it out loud?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: "To the SRK command, based to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters have the proper page in English, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Based on the oral --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you now please look at item 12? We are talking about November and December 1994 and it shows the consumption, and item 2 is aerial bombs. It says, "3 pieces." Were you aware that sometime in November or December 1994, three aerial bombs were used? Did you know anything at all about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't. I was living at the time in Pale, as I said. I was a civilian. And I had no way of knowing whether this was used or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So what happened next during 1995, after this offensive was mounted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you going to ask the witness about the source of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is document 65 ter, and the source, I think, should be explained by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Who signed it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That is something that I omitted to ask.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document was signed by Lieutenant-Colonel Milivoje Solar assistant commander for logistics. And he sent this document to the assistant commander of logistics. Mr. Milivoje Solar was stationed in Lukavica and the command post, the rear command post, was at Pale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Chairman, Mr. Chairman, I'm sorry, there is a serious mistake. It's on page 20, line 10. The rear command post was in Pale. [Interpretation] The witness didn't speak about this. He said the command post of logistics, not the rear command post. And it's not quite the same. The rear command post but not in Pale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have noticed that same mistake earlier on in the transcripts and I suspect it will be corrected later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't realise it popped up earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Since His Honour, Judge Robinson, asked a question relating to this document, in your opinion, the document as it is with the letterhead and the signature and the contents, is something that you have no doubts about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I don't. It's been properly registered. It's been signed, and I have no doubts about this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you then please explain this to the Judges? What was the situation in May, June, July, in the wake of the conflicts or actually what were the conflicts like at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conflicts started on the 16th of June 1995, when the BH army attacked Iljas, Vogosca, and they were the fiercest ones from the beginning of the war. According to the information obtained by the army of Republika Srpska, the strongest forces were brought to the positions of the BH army from all of their units. In the previous six months or a year, I watched on the BH television reports provided by certain officers about the attacks. My personal opinion, and thanks to the command of General Milosevic, the positions of the units in -- of Republika Srpska army in the region of Sarajevo were defended. If you ask me how do I know that it was precisely the 16th, I remember that day because that was my wife's birthday, and they attacked Vogosca, Iljas, on that day. After that the attacks were shifted to the area of Kijevo near Trnovo, then to the area of Zlatiste and Lukavica. In all these places, the BH army initially shifted their lines. However, owing to the engagement of the personnel who were defending their homes and their families, the BH army forces were repelled in these first two days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, can I just ask you one additional question in relation to the attack of the ABiH in June 1995? Did you have any information about the reasons why the ABiH launched this attack? What was the purpose of the attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The BH army had their own objectives. A unified Bosnia-Herzegovina with no Serbs in it. They wanted to beat the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, conquer the territory defended by the Serbs who had lived in the area for centuries. If you want more information, I'll be happy to provide it. Look at my family. We had lived in this place since 1880, according to official information. I at one point drew up a family tree and I know this. We have been living in the same place for the last 130 years. The address changed many times, but the place remains essentially the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I have no doubt about the right of the Serbs to remain in the areas which they have inhabited. That's not the issue. The issue is whether you were aware or whether you had gathered intelligence or knew of any intelligence that had been gathered about the specific situation in Sarajevo, because I assume that what you just told me or told the Chamber was the general purpose of the ABiH. But what was the specific purpose of these attacks in relation to the situation in Sarajevo? That was my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My answer to that question is this: The BH army was out to beat the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps in order to attain its objectives. I don't know about their specific objectives. I think they should know, not me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If Your Honour, Judge Harhoff, has finished with his question, perhaps I was going to ask you, but I don't think there is any point now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this instead: How did the civilians feel, the people behind the lines held by the army of Republika Srpska, civilians in their flats, houses, with their children, families, what exactly were those people feeling? And if you could also tell us what the civilians in Sarajevo itself were feeling at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you about the civilians in the Serb parts. My family, my neighbours, were all concerned about what was going on. They were all concerned about their lives. However, everyone down to the last man were determined to fight and defend what was theirs. Throughout the war, most of the population never left their homes at all. They were perfectly capable of defending their own homes, and they were prepared to sacrifice their lives to avoid leaving their respective areas. The same thing happened during the June 1995 attack. All the forces were concentrated on defending the Serb areas and that's why the areas were eventually defended, for that reason alone. There were other areas where units from other corps came and those units sometime abandoned their positions. Everyone rose to defend the Serb positions, from those aged 18 to senior citizens who were still strong enough to carry a weapon. Rest assured that this was the only reason that the area was actually defended. The BH army operations were incredible, mind boggling, the fiercest since the beginning of the war. Only those who were determined to defend their homes could remain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you told us about what those people were feeling. I wasn't going to ask you about this but still, were there any casualties among the soldiers and civilians in the places that you went, where you were or your position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course there were casualties. Back in May, when the first attack was launched, I went back home to see how my family were doing. Just below the fort at Zlatiste. I saw that hundreds of shells had fallen, launched by the Muslims. Just outside my home, I was looking at this, and I could not understand how they had got hold of all the ammunition given the problems that we had with ammunition shortage. I don't know how they got their ammunition, but I know that their supplies at the time were far better than ours. I don't have any information to indicate that to any degree of specificity. But what I saw there and then would seem to suggest that they had enormous amounts of ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right, witness. You're telling me about ammunition, and I'm asking you about human lives. What about casualties among soldiers and civilians to the extent that you were able to observe?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Reports on those killed never reached my department, my service, but I know that on the 17th of June, at one point in time, during that morning, five soldiers were killed along the front line. Two of those were my relatives. There were other civilians who were killed, but I'm hard put to tell you anything about those. I wasn't there and my information is hardly appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just to wrap this up, can you tell us what happened in August, September, October? What exactly happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In late August -- you're probably going to laugh, but I was off to my honeymoon on the 29th of August. The 30th of August is my birthday. So just the day before my birthday, we were off on our honeymoon in Montenegro. During our stay there, swift intervention units attacked, units of the corps. After I was back from the sea coast, I reassured myself that nobody was hurt among my neighbours but the -- substantial material damage had occurred. I got my orders to make an assessment of damage to the buildings inside the Lukavica barracks. I don't have the information at my fingertips but I know that damage was severe, especially that which occurred to maintenance buildings where we repaired vehicles. There was one particular building in the Lukavica barracks where vehicle repairs were being carried out and there was a lot of damage there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you finally tell me this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I was going to ask you to remind us again how you weave all these attacks by the Serb forces into the defence, into your case. It's very important for me to understand it and as you go along, I am trying to work it out, you know? It seems to me, and you have said this before, that what you are saying is that it's not just that the -- sorry, the ABiH forces were responsible for attacks, but that the attacks with which the Serb forces are charged in the indictment leading to the charges of murder as a crime against humanity, inhumane acts, a crime against humanity, and so on, that the Serb forces, in all cases, acted responsively to attacks by the ABiH and that is how we arrive at the allegations made by the Prosecution. Because, of course, you know that it's not sufficient to show that the ABiH forces also committed crimes. So I presume you're going further than that, and it is -- it is in that area that I am seeking clarification and I'm only seeking clarification in trying to understand how the defence is putting its case. So we have just listened to the witness narrate a series of attacks by the ABiH forces, and in some cases he did speak of the Serbs defending their positions, defending themselves. But can you just let me know again how the case is being put?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will try to be as brief as possible since my time is running out, and I'm going to try to reply to this. You know that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Explanation that you give in response to a question like this will not count against your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I think I should tell you right now, if we look at the indictment, and I don't have one handy, the most important count is the fact that the army of Republika Srpska had a single objective, that of killing civilians, deliberately, by design and by direct targeting. The most important thing being its objective was to spread terror among the civilian population. My -- I have told you a number of times and needless to say, I will always try and explain this. What exactly the situation was between the beginning of August and the end of 1994?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Sachdeva?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm terribly sorry to interrupt but I was wondering if my learned friend was going to be providing an answer to your question that this could be done in the absence of the witness, lest there be any possibility for prejudice before my cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't see the need for that, Mr. Sachdeva. You have seen this done before in the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I have actually in the previous case that I worked on, the Galic case, I know that when issues of substance were discussed which impacted directly on witnesses' testimony, sometimes the witness would be asked both by the Defence and the Prosecution to be taken out of the courtroom. It's simply a submission, and I obviously defer to your rulings. But it has been done in the past in my experience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I will not follow that practice in this case because I frankly don't see the need for it. So I'm going to ask Mr. Tapuskovic just to explain briefly the situation that I raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in our view, and this is something that we were going to show during our case, there was a peaceful period between the end of December and May or June, during which there were few incidents, and one certainly couldn't say that anyone at all was subjected to terror in that period. If we speak of terror in the circumstances of a war such as this one, then this terror can't be in one area and not in another. As we keep adducing evidence, I will show you how terror was forced on the Serb population outside these areas, and this cannot be considered a tu quoque. There was terror on both sides in both population groups; fear of war, everybody wanted the war to stop, but the war was renewed in the most intensive way possible in May and June not thanks to any efforts on the part of the army of Republika Srpska. And atrocities continued because of these renewed operations. By this time there would probably be no more fear, no more terror, had the offensive by the BH army not taken on these dimensions. Whatever the BH army did throughout this period of time, and I'm not talking about any time before this, I'm looking at the period and the circumstances under which Mr. Dragomir Milosevic operated at the time and particularly during this specific offensive, there were not sufficient weapons, there was no ammunition, there was only the hope that whatever was done was done in extreme necessity, and the hope that no one would be jeopardised by direct targeting. I will be dealing with each of the incidents separately stated in the indictment, saying that crimes were perpetrated by direct firing, directly targeting the civilians. We will be dealing with that and I'm sure that we shall be successful in proving that in most cases it was not proved beyond a reasonable doubt that the incidents were committed the way that it is claimed. As for terror, that prevailed throughout the war, this was due to a fierce offensive launched by the BH army and nothing else. Had that not occurred, the war would probably have been over by May any way, possibly even earlier, regardless of any strategic political and historical circumstances surrounding this situation, which is not something that I'll be dwelling on. The facts of the case are peace had been going on for sometime and had this offensive not occurred, it would have stayed like that. Any reaction was absolutely called for. There had to be some reaction. They couldn't just sit on their hands. But the objective of this reaction was not to threaten anyone or put anyone's lives at risk, as to any forms that occurred later on or whatever may have happened --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: From what you have said, I think the important submission is that as for terror that prevailed throughout the war this was due to a fierce offensive launched by the army and nothing else. I presume you mean launched by the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time, certainly, had it not been for that offensive nothing else would have happened. The previous five months, according to our information, had been filled with peace. No incidents. In the autumn of 1994, when offensives occurred and clashes occurred along front lines that were remote and far from any urban centres. There were sporadic acts of provocation more than anything. So that is what really characterises that period of time, and the army of Republika Srpska didn't do much. Some say it's because they'd already taken by this time what they were aiming at. But there was no option at this time and witnesses will show this to launch any sort of action at all. The objective was to simply remain where they were and that was about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before you move on, I just want to correct something. When I started by asking the question I referred to the Serb forces, and the reference should have been to the BiH forces. Please continue. And please note that you are now beyond the time that had been allocated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Robinson, I am glad that I had another opportunity to say it in response to your request and it is my duty to offer this kind of explanation. However, I think that in redirect, I will have an opportunity to clear and clarify some things with the witness. I wanted to show him certain documents, but I think we should leave it for a later stage and at this point I would like to finish my examination and give the floor to my learned colleague, the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we just have two minutes. We'll take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Good morning, to you Witness. My name is Manoj Sachdeva and I am a lawyer for the Prosecution, and I will ask you some questions today. You know that you have protective measures, so I will refer to you as T-53 or Witness. Just to start with, is it possible to have that document, the previous document, up on the screen again, please? Witness, Defence counsel just showed you this document, and I recall that in your evidence, you said that this was a correct and valid document from the SRK; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only say that I'm looking at a report which was compiled in keeping within the regulations. As for the accuracy, I wouldn't know. I was not there at that moment, and I can't tell you whether this is accurate or not. But judging by everything I see, it should be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And if we can just scroll down to the bottom on the English version, the signature there -- perhaps we can go into private session, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, I just want to get a proper understanding of your movements from May 1992 throughout the conflict. You told the Court that you moved from various places to various places. I understand that on the 28th of May in 1992, you were posted at Lukavica barracks for about 15 days; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And after that, you moved to a place called Tilava, am I right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And then from September 1992 through to 1st of April 1994, you were at Pale?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the facility that you've mentioned, which is Turist hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Right. And then after that from the 1st of April 1994 up until January 1995 or December 1994, you told the Court that you went back to the factory that you used to work for before the war, and am I correct in saying that would be the Famos factory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have enough time to explain things to Mr. Tapuskovic's question. Two or three years before the war, the car factory in Sarajevo was split into several facilities. And when this happened, I became affiliated with the factory of special vehicles. I returned to that factory. It's very difficult to explain. And those people who lived there didn't understand it. I did not want to go into that much detail in front of the Court. So the correct -- the accurate name of that factory would be the factory of special vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Was that factory at the Famos location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That factory -- actually, Famos was located in several places. Most of it was in the locality call Hrasnica, in the lower part of the eastern Sarajevo. Whereas another part of the factory, the overhaul part of the factory, was in Pale. In 1994, from the 1st of April to the end of that year, I spent in Pale. This is where I resided. I resided in Pale. I got married when I did, as I've told you, which took place in Grbavica. I would go there occasionally, maybe once or twice in a fortnight, to see my parents, and then I would return to Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Just continuing with the Famos factory in Hrasnica. Through your work, were you aware of what was made in that factory at Famos in that period, 1994-1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no production in the Famos at that time. The separation line between the army of Republika Srpska and the BiH army went through the factory itself at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Nevertheless, the Famos factory was controlled by the VRS in that period, was it not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the separation line went through the Famos perimeter. One part of the facility was under the control of the BH army and the other under the control of the VRS army. On the 7th of April 1992, was the last time when I was in that part of the factory where I had worked. On that day, I took my leave, and I never returned to the factory until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Did you hear during your time at the factory and also after the conflict broke out that optical sights for rifles were produced at the Famos factory? Did you ever hear that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Famos never produced optical sights for the rifles. Maybe I could tell you where they were produced. Would you be interested in that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Why don't you tell the Court where they were produced.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Optical sights were produced in the Zrak factory in Sarajevo which was under the control of BiH army. Famos never manufactured optical sights, never ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, I want to concentrate on your time at the Lukavica barracks from January 1995 through to, I understand, the end of August 1995. That's the time you were there, was it not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not completely correct. I was there until the end of the war. Until the moment the command of the Sarajevo Corps was moved to Pale, and I don't know the exact date. From the 1st of January 1995 up to sometime in December 1995, I would say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, may I ask you about the evidence that you gave concerning the optical sights being produced not in the Famos factory but at a factory in Sarajevo that was under the control of the BiH army? What period is this that you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Zrak factory in Sarajevo, I don't know when it was incepted, but my late cousin -- up to 1992, I'm sure. I don't know what was going on in the war. I was never at that factory, but I know that up to 1992 it manufactured optical sights for the army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And do you know who manufactured optical sights for the Serb army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether they were produced at all. Any production is not under the control of the army but of the Ministry of Defence. Whether optical sights were produced or not, I can't tell you. There was a factory before the war which served the needs of the entire state of Yugoslavia and during the war it was under the control of the BiH army. Whether they continued their production during the war I can't tell you. Before the war they did produce optical sights.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, I was just asking you about your time at the SRK command Lukavica barracks from January through to the end of the war, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I feel we need to go into private session again, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, how many floors did the Lukavica barracks have?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm asking you how many storeys or floors did the Lukavica barracks have.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Lukavica barracks occupies an area of approximately 100 hectares, approximately. I'm not an expert, but I would say that that is the area. And there are several buildings in that area. I wouldn't know their number. So we can't talk about any floors.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Wasn't the operations department or the operations room on the ground floor of the barracks? Is that right? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that either I am getting a wrong interpretation or your questions are rather imprecise. I don't know what the problem is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether the operations department of the SRK command was in the ground floor of the barracks. If you don't know, that's fine. If you do know, please tell me the answer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, you're very imprecise. The operations centre of the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was on the ground floor of a building, not in the barracks. A barracks is a rather large term where a building is just one facility, one building.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So it was in the building that housed the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And it was in the same building that Dragomir Milosevic had his office; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And Mr. Krsmanovic's unit, that is your unit, was that in the same building, too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Where was that office?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That unit was located in the Turist Hotel in Pale. That's where its base was. I and Lieutenant-Colonel Solar shared an office in a building in the Lukavica barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And Mr. Krsmanovic, was he also in that building or are you saying that he was at Pale?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: During 1995, I saw Mr. Krsmanovic maybe on three or four occasions. We did not share the same location. He was in command of the rear echelon from the Turist hotel in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Did yourself or Mr. Solar participate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President. Just one thing regarding once again the rear echelon in the Turist hotel, because even Judge Harhoff realised that there was a confusion systematically so between logistics and what could be that echelon which is behind or sort of shifted compared to the normal command post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So what are you saying should be the translation?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as far as I'm concerned, in English, I would say, "the logistics command post," but I'm not an expert. It's not the same. There are two different terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sachdeva?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Perhaps we can move into closed session -- private session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, okay now I'm understanding. Your office was on the same floor as the general, General Milosevic. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And what floor was that? Can you tell the Court? Was it the second floor? Was it the first floor? Of that building.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The building had a ground floor and the first floor, and we were located on the first floor of that building, on the first floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So that would be the top floor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the top floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And when you went into the office of Dragomir Milosevic, General Milosevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't know the period of time that is being dealt with when we're talking about all this. What period of time is my learned friend referring to? Four years is a rather long period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sachdeva? What period of time does this relate to?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I started asking the witness about his time at Lukavica barracks, when he was stationed there from January 1995 through to the end of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, you told the Court earlier that -- in response to a question from the President about air bombs, you told the Court that you heard about these bombs from the Muslim press, being fired into Sarajevo. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not from the press. We did not receive any press. I said that I heard it on the Muslim radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And when you went into General Milosevic's office, did he also have such means available, i.e. a radio and a television? Were those contraptions present at the office?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I've told you that I heard that at the beginning of July 1995. I had a car radio. In my car, I had a radio, and I heard it on the radio. I don't know what Mr. Milosevic heard or what others had. I can only tell you what I heard. He may have heard it himself. Maybe not. I'm a witness. I have declared that I would speak the truth and that's what I'm telling you. I can't share anybody else's truth with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm not asking you what General Milosevic heard. I'm simply asking you that in his office was there a television in his office?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so. After such a long time, after 12 or 13 years, I can't tell you whether there was a TV set. Maybe there was. There probably was. And at times there was electricity and at times there wasn't. That's all that I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I understand that from General Milosevic's office there was a view from his window on the city of Sarajevo, particularly Dobrinja; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know. I believe that from his office, you could not see Dobrinja. You may be could see just one corner of Dobrinja, but I would have to go back to that office to see exactly what he could see. From my windows, I could see Mojmilo and I can't really tell you what one could see from his window. It was on the other side of the building and his office was facing Mount Igman. I really can't tell you with any certainty whether he could see even a corner of Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Presumably, though, as you've testified that you used to go into his office, if there were, when bombs used to fall on Sarajevo, and in Dobrinja, Mr. Milosevic would have been able to see the effects of those bombs, that is the smoke rising from the ground; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I've told you I never saw a bomb, a shell. I never saw any action by shelling. I told you what I had heard. I was not in such places where I could see any bombs. And as for Mr. Milosevic, whether he saw something or not, I really can't tell you. I can't speak on behalf of anybody else. Can I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You were not being asked that. As I understand it, you were being asked to say whether based on the knowledge, the familiarity that you had with Mr. Milosevic's office, whether Mr. Milosevic would have been able to see the bombs, the effects of the bombs, and the smoke rising from the ground, from his office.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think so. I don't think he could see anything from that office. Behind the building where the command was located there was a theatre. The building had only one floor, one floor and a half, and I really can't tell you what exactly he could see from there. I believe that he could not see much from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, we spoke earlier about these meetings at the command and of course, you told the Court that you wouldn't attend, but did the persons that attended these meetings, did they ever discuss with you the subject matter of these meetings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am a desk officer. What the chiefs were talking about at the meetings, there is a principle of subordination in the military and the chain of command is very well known. You have a commander, chief of departments and then further on. If you think that some of these chiefs talked about something, there was no need for that. I had my chief, I was accountable to him. He gave me orders and I carried orders. That's how it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You were a desk officer, that's right but you also drafted or requested documents for General Milosevic; did you not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, based on the requests from subordinate units of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, based on their requests, the requests were forwarded to the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska. Based on the Main Staff's orders, ammunition was taken over in -- during a certain period, the logistics organ of the SRK had a small ammunition depot under their control and from that depot they could directly distribute ammunition to certain units.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And some of these requests were signed and sent out by the commander, General Milosevic; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is obvious that a commander issues orders. Certain things that he ordered that related to the logistics I may have seen; I may not have seen. I cannot tell you now. But in principle, some of the documents were sent to the logistics command post at Pale, and some we -- some documents were -- Colonel Solar and I were familiar with, probably containing the information that Commander Milosevic thought we should know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: In fact, General Milosevic ensured that he knew precisely the requests that were going out to the Main Staff and it was him that made -- that gave the orders for the distribution of weapons within his command, within his corps, within the SRK; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He gave orders on rare occasions. In the majority of cases, as far as I know, the orders for distribution of ammunition were issued by Colonel Aleksa Krsmanovic. Also, the Chief of the Technical Service, Mr. Antun Sinkovic, or the Chief of the Operations and Logistics, Mr. Solar, could have issued these orders, but that was in most cases. The war ended 12 years ago. You should understand that. And I cannot tell you exactly who signed the documents. Whatever was under the jurisdiction of the logistics was signed by the Assistant Commander for Logistics, Mr. Aleksa Krsmanovic. In his absence, someone else may have signed the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Let's talk about Mr. Krsmanovic. You knew him well, did you not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I take it that he took his job and responsibility seriously and professionally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is difficult for me to say at this moment. I expected you to ask me that. It is not very nice to speak ill about your superior. After his son was killed in 1992, Mr. Krsmanovic acted strangely at times. His son was killed in 1992, and I'm telling you that after that, Mr. Krsmanovic behaved strangely in certain periods.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: He remained the commander of the unit up until the end of the war, did he not, within the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, the commander of your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And as far as you were aware, when you had dealings with him, he was a professional?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a communications officer per establishment and he worked in the personnel department. He came to us from the personnel department as a third commander. The first commander was Colonel Bosko Pasic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down when listing names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, Witness. You're speaking too fast. The interpreter is having difficulty following you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, I'm sorry, I'm going to interrupt you, but I want us to concentrate on Mr. Krsmanovic in his role as the commander of your unit up until the end of the war. Now, it is right, is it not, that Mr. Krsmanovic, in taking his job seriously, would have to be aware of all the ammunition requests that came to him and he would have to understand fully the workings of his unit? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He should have known. All these documents should have arrived on his desk, as he was assistant commander for logistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And in his role he would have had regular communication or in fact meetings with General Milosevic; isn't that also right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer this question. I don't know how often they were in touch. I said that in 1995, I didn't see Colonel Aleksa Krsmanovic more than five or six times, ten at the most. He was in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm not asking you what you know and what you saw. I'm simply asking you in terms of the hierarchy, that his role, the role that he occupied, would have necessitated regular meetings with the general and the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, so far we have adhered to a rule that when something is being put to a witness, that he first be told what kind of document is in question, where something is being read from, before reading the document itself. We didn't hear at all what this is all about. What document are we talking about? What statement? When was it given and by whom? And only after that can something be read out loud. This is how we practised during these proceedings. However, Mr. Sachdeva started reading immediately something. We, as the witness, don't know what the document in question is. I think it would have been more appropriate to tell the witness what the document is and then ask him to comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He did say that this was a statement to the Bosnian authorities in February 1996. Perhaps a little more would be quite in order.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: As you've ordered, Mr. President. But also I fear that -- are we in open session? I fear that we need to go into private session and possibly the last paragraph should be redacted. I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session, then.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, it may be the case that brigade commanders could redeploy weapons to another brigade within the SRK. However, you would agree that the general, General Milosevic, would have been informed of that redeployment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot answer that question. I was not an officer and there was no need for me to be involved in that. I didn't receive this type of information. I was never in contact with the officers in charge of other affairs such as deployment of equipment, et cetera. I don't know where weapons of the army of Republika Srpska or the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps were deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: But, Witness, did you not sign documents on behalf of General Dragomir Milosevic with respect to the deployment of weaponry or requests for weaponry? You did that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, and if my memory serves me well, I didn't sign a single document during the war. I cannot be categorical. It lasted for four years. But there were so many superior officers who signed the documents. It wasn't my duty to do so, especially not on behalf of General Milosevic. He had his staff, and I was very low down the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Actually, I apologise. What I actually meant to ask you was that you drafted documents for Dragomir Milosevic. You may not have signed them, but you drafted documents for Dragomir Milosevic's signature. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the documents relating to the logistics, that is to the supply of units, it did happen that I prepared some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I'm going to show you some documents now for the next ten or 15 minutes or so, but before I do that I wanted to talk to you about your evidence with respect to the weaponry the ABiH had and the weaponry the SRK had. You recall that you told the Court just before I started examining you that you went to where you used to live, I recall, in May 1995, and you said that you saw the results of a hundred shells falling in that area. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you also said that you were surprised that the ABiH had that many weapons. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: But you never saw any document, or you never came across any evidence that suggested the ABiH were superior in terms of weaponry, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't see any documents, but I saw with my own eyes these hundreds -- I didn't count them- - but a larger quantity of heavy artillery weapons that fell at 100 metres from my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Let's just stick to what I asked you, please. And I think you've confirmed your answer that you never saw any document. In fact, you told the Court when you went to Lukavica barracks in May 1992 that the weapons that were contained in the barracks were -- in fact, you said there were a great number of tanks and howitzers and heavy weaponry. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you also know that the factory of Pretis was controlled by the VRS; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And the factory of Pretis produced weapons and ammunition for the SRK, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The factory of Pretis produced ammunition, not weapons. It produced ammunition and for 50 years before the war, it worked to meet the needs of the former state. That is why it was established and that is what it produced before the war. It did have some production during the war, but these were minor quantities, negligible quantities, compared to what it did before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm only asking you about the war, the time during the war, and it's correct that the Pretis factory produced ammunition for the SRK, that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will give you an answer to this question. According to its position and state Vogosca was not under the jurisdiction of the SRK. Its a factory that operated on economic principles. In order for it to survive it needed money. Please allow me to give you an answer. I will answer your question. It was under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Defence of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm not asking you under whose jurisdiction it was, I'm simply asking you whether the factory at Pretis produced weapons for the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. That's all I'm asking you. Do you agree or disagree?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The interpreters are not translating properly. Not weapons. I said ammunition. Pretis did not produce weapons. It produced ammunition for the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you also know that in May 1992, the warehouse at Faletici, the majority of weapons that were contained in that warehouse were taken over by the VRS; that's correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer that question. I was in a different place at the time. I said that on the 28th of May 1992, I became a member of the logistics organ. And I didn't receive any information of that nature at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You never heard that was the case in spite of the fact that you weren't there, you never heard that? You never heard that the Faletici warehouse was guarded by JNA guards in that period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no need for me to know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And the 27th logistics base was in Sokolac, was it not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Its headquarters was in Sokolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you said that it supplied the ammunition and weapons to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and the Drina Corps; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So it's correct that the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps had access to ammunition and weapons from a variety of sources; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one can say that but in principle, if you allow me, I can clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'd just simply want you to answer the question: Did they have access or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Part of the ammunition, at the time when there were no combat activities, the logistics organ of the command of the SRK kept the ammunition in their warehouse within the compound of the 27th logistics base in Pale. So for the most part, the ammunition depot was in Pale, in the Jahorinski Potok barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, we need to go into private session. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, I am -- I apologise for all the procedural discussions, and I'm going to go back to my question just so you can refresh your memory. Again, it is a question that has been asked by the Presiding Judge in the Galic case, His Honour Judge Orie, to your supervisor, and Judge Orie asked your supervisor, and I quote, "I'm not asking about ... but specialised warehouses where greater amounts of ammunition and/or weaponry was stored. You told us about Faletici and how it went with Faletici, but similar warehouses of similar sizes, were they also within BiH-held territory? And your supervisor answered, as far as I know they weren't. There wasn't such big warehouses in Sarajevo." And I'm asking you would you agree with that testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not relation to this particular case. May I clarify?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is my own experience. I saw ammunition that they used to fire, the stories about there not being any warehouses. You can set up a warehouse in any basement. They obviously had far more ammunition than we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, let me put it this way. This is something that you are assuming, you don't know, do you? This is based on your assumptions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you I'm a civilian. I wasn't privy to the number or location of warehouses, ammunition warehouses, in Sarajevo. I'm still not. There were the police as well, and they had their own police warehouses. Other people would be better placed to know that sort of thing. I certainly wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Very well, you don't know, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'd now like to bring up a document, it's 65 ter 03217. And perhaps rather than going into private session, we could just ensure that the document is not broadcast. Witness, do you see a document there on your screen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you see that this is a document that emanates from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you see at the bottom that it is signed by your colleague?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you would agree that this is a valid and authentic document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I have a look first, go through the document so that I may actually address it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You may look at that but just -- I'm asking you with respect to the form and -- the form, does it appear to you to be an authentic document from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as its form is concerned, I'd say yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And if you look at the list of ammunition that has been ordered to be delivered to the 3rd Sarajevo Brigade, if you see down the list --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've had a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You see that it talks about 40 pieces for a mortar, an 82 millimetre mortar, do you see that there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you know that 82 millimetre mortars are weaponry that -- that is heavy and also part of the weapons exclusion zone agreement. You know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Prosecutor, you obviously don't see the date on this document when this document was produced. It's the 16th of June 1995. On that day, the BH army attacked the positions of the army of Republika Srpska with everything they had. Only a stupid person would not use any weapons they had to defend themselves from an enemy attack. You had to use everything that you had to defend from the BH army attacks. This 82 millimetre mortar, it's a play thing as compared to everything else that was actually used in that war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you also see that there was a request for 13.200 pieces of 6.62 millimetre bullets and 5.400 pieces for 7.9 millimetre sniper bullets? You see that there as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you also see that the paragraph at the bottom, it specifically states, that these quantities of ammunition are intended for units of the SRK at the northwestern part of Sarajevo war theatre and it cannot be issued without the personal approval of the corps commander, the corps commander being General Milosevic; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And Mr. President, I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We admit it and we'll take a break.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be admitted as P766.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic? You have a point to pick?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, let me tell you something about the time for this witness. He has to travel today. He's been here for a week. And I believe that we should bear in mind the time that the Prosecution still has. In my view they have already spent all their time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva, of the time allocated to you, you have another ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would ask your leave to go beyond the ten minutes, if possible. In the Prosecution's submission, there are several documents that he would have been privy to that, in my submission, are important for Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And how much beyond the ten minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think I would require another 20 to 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. Yes. That would give us enough time because the re-examination, I don't imagine, would be unduly long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Be as fast as you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. Could we now have 65 ter 02319 brought up on the screen and again not to be broadcast, please. That appears to be the wrong document. It's 65 ter 03219. Yes, that's the one. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, do you see a document there on your screen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Again, can you confirm that this is, in its form it is an authentic document from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In its form, yes, but it hasn't been signed by Mr. Milosevic. I'm not familiar with the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And the document is a request for ammunition for combat actions, is it not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And at the bottom of the page, General Dragomir Milosevic's name is there, as a commander, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And do you see the initials SM? I take it that this was drafted by your colleague? Don't mention the name because we are in open session but --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you see that General Dragomir Milosevic has asked the VRS Main Staff to supply the SRK with, amongst other things, 200 pieces of 76 millimetre bullets. Do you see that there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: 600 pieces for an 82 millimetre mortar? That's number 3?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And at the bottom, we see in number 15 and 16, we see the request for in total 30 pieces of FAB aerial bombs. Do you see that there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, in your evidence-in-chief to -- when were you asked questions about air bombs by Mr. Tapuskovic, your evidence was that at that time I knew and this was in early June 1995, you say that you knew there was no need for these type of weapons; that is air bombs. Do you remember saying that in evidence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So I take it then that your evidence is that General Dragomir Milosevic is asking for weapons that he does not intend to use? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. This was signed by another person. And the request was made to the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska. This is a request.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, we can see that it is a request but I'm asking you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: -- given your work in this unit and your knowledge of this issue, it is not the case, is it, that General Milosevic would be asking for weapons he does not intend to use? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that. I was not the one to decide what would be used. You have to ask somebody else. A request was indeed made for this type ammunition. I will subscribe to that but that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And witness, you know that at this time in fact your evidence has been that there was intensive combat operations ongoing in Sarajevo. That's right, is it not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Is it also right that General Milosevic would not have the time to request for specific weapons if he did not intend to use them? In other words, he would not be making frivolous requests, would he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, sir, if you had been there at the time, you would have addressed St. Peter to help you. We were attacked by a corps with the strongest units from other corps, and you would you ask for anything that could be of assistance in defending yourself. After this request, I don't know whether this was approved or not. I don't know what happened next. I see that the document was signed by somebody. I don't know that my colleague from the office --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva and Mr. Tapuskovic, there is a matter I wish to bring to your attention. Number 15 on the B/C/S has FAB 105, and then 20. Number 15 in the English translation has FAB and then italicised, "aerial bombs." So the question is -- what explains this inconsistency? You may not be able to explain it, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, the term FAB is a Russian abbreviation and it stands for Fugasnaya Avionskaya Bomba.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Which means?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Which, in my submission, means aerial bomb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I believe you qualify now for the Russian booth, if we had one, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'll ask the witness some questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, you have earlier said in your evidence that the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps did not have aircraft. You remember telling the Court that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So you would agree that these FAB aerial bombs would not have been dropped from planes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And in your time at the Sarajevo command, when you worked there, it's correct, isn't it, that these air bombs were modified by way of attaching rockets to the bombs and they were launched from trucks, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that question. I performed my duties in my office. I did not fire a single bullet during the war let alone having been in a position from which fire was opened and especially from pieces like this. I did not need to inspect any positions. That was not my duty. I performed my duties, and I told you exactly what those duties were. And I'm not familiar with this at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, I didn't ask you whether you fired bullets during the war, which is what you have told the Court. I'm asking you whether you know whether these air bombs were modified for use at the city of Sarajevo. What do you say about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Are you saying you can't answer it because you don't want to, or you can't answer it because you don't know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You know, though, that these air bombs were -- firstly you know that they were requested by the commander of the SRK, that's clear, is it not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And it's also clear that he -- they would not be able to be dropped on Sarajevo by airplanes, you will agree with that as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you agree that they were modified, therefore, for their deployment, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that this document be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P767, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I also ask now, again not to be broadcast, that 65 ter 02557 be brought up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, there is another document on your screen. And again, can you confirm that it emanates from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can the document be scrolled down, please, so I can see its entirety? In form, it seems to be all right, but I can't see the signature, I don't know who signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'll show you the signature in a moment, if we can just go back up to the top, please. Witness, if you look at the top you'll see that it was dated on the 27th of July 1995. You see that there, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And again, well, I can show you the signature, if we go to the next page. You see General Milosevic's name there, don't you, as the commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And again, the initials SM refer to your colleague that we spoke about earlier? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And he drafted this document, did he not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you would agree with me that this is a request for again replenishment of ammunition to be used by units engaged in combat? You agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-53 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And if we go back to the first page, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Who signed the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, do you know whose signature that is?
